Xbox has been on a slow decline since the botched Xbox One launch in 2013. The exclusives have started disappearing, the hardware stopped mattering, and now a third price increase in a year puts the Series X at $800.

When Sony raised PS5 prices, Xbox had an open lane. Undercut them and the average consumer picks the cheaper console. Instead they matched the increase and handed the advantage right back to Sony.

Their biggest franchise is also about to be on PlayStation next month. None of this is how a company behaves when it wants to sell consoles. 

I hate to say this, but I believe we're witnessing the death of the Xbox in real time.

People are finding out the hard way that buying digital isn't buying, it's renting.

Every disc, tape, and cartridge I own still works. No matter how many licenses expire, no corporation can reach into my house and take it back.

That's the entire argument for physical media, sitting right there in that email.

Batman Arkham Knight, June 22, 2015.

Grown adults lined up down the sidewalk of the strip mall to get a video game. 

There was a real sense of community. Everyone out interacting, having a good time.

Digital killed all of that.

E3 2013. 

Microsoft told everyone the Xbox One would require online check-ins and lock down used games. 

Then Sony walked out, put this on the screen, and the place lost its mind.

Trade it.
Sell it. 
Lend it.  
Keep it forever. 

PlayStation won that entire generation on one promise: the disc is yours.

Worth remembering who we were cheering for, and what they were promising.

I've taken a lot of heat the last few days for being pro physical media.

It's a crazy thing to insult someone over, but here's the actual reason, and it has nothing to do with discs versus downloads.

It's the memories.

Playing the Mario games with my mom on the NES 35+ years ago. 

My parents taking me to Toys R Us to pick out a Nintendo game for my birthday. 

The first time I ever beat a game on my own, Yoshi's Island on the SNES in 1995. 

The time I got suspended for fighting and my mom took me to Blockbuster to rent RoboCop vs Terminator anyway. 

Sneaking into my aunt's room to play Sonic on her Sega Genesis in the middle of the night on a school night.

Opening a brand new game, pulling out the manual, unfolding the poster that came inside and hanging it on my bedroom wall.

Digital is easier, faster, cleaner. I know. But a download doesn't carry any of that. A cartridge does.

That's what I'm holding onto. Not the plastic. The memory attached to it.

Go all digital and the next kid never gets any of this. Just a license that disappears when someone decides it should.

Honest and Unpopular Reviews No. 5 
The Legend of Zelda (NES)

This game invented an entire genre and is heralded as one of the greatest games of all time.

The opening hours are slow, and the game gives you almost nothing to go on. Entire dungeons and critical items are hidden behind burning a random bush or bombing an unmarked wall.

Back in the late 80s, you didn't figure that out on your own. You figured it out with a Nintendo Power magazine, a friend at school, or a call to the Nintendo hotline.

The Legend of Zelda gets a 4 out of 5 rating from me.

Honest and Unpopular Reviews No. 7
R.C. Pro-Am (NES)

Most people remember this one fondly and then leave it out of every serious racing conversation. I think that's a mistake. This is a top 5 racing game of all time.

Rare had weapons, upgrades, and rubber-band AI figured out four years before kart racers got credit for inventing any of it. The drift handling still feels good today, and collecting letters to spell NINTENDO for the next car was a progression hook nobody else had in 1988.

It's more fun than Mario Kart. It's more fun than Gran Turismo. It's miles ahead of Forza.

It loses a point for repetition. The tracks start blurring together deep into the circuit, and that yellow car cheats like it's getting paid to.

I rate this one a 4 out of 5.

Minimalism is one of the worst lifestyle trends of my lifetime and I'm glad I escaped it.

Over 15 years ago I bought into the concept. Boxed up almost everything and put it in storage. Kept a handful of current gen games on the shelf, a couple of posters on the wall, and that was it. Own less, be free, all of that.

And for a while I told myself it felt good. Clean surfaces. Nothing extra.

It only took a couple of years to break. I started missing things. Actual things sitting in boxes in a storage unit. Games. Movies. Stuff with history attached to it. 

And I started noticing something else: everything around me had no character.

My space looked like a rental listing. Beige, empty, and cold. It could have belonged to anyone, which meant it belonged to no one.

That's the part nobody tells you about minimalism. It doesn't just remove clutter. It removes evidence that you exist. Every shelf you empty is a story you can't tell anymore.

So I went the other way. Pulled things out of boxes. Started collecting again. Started enjoying things again.

Now I sit in a room surrounded by 30+ years of games, consoles, and memories, and it feels more like freedom than an empty room ever did.

Keep your history.
Keep your hobbies.
Keep the stuff that makes your space yours.

That's not clutter. That's character.

Bill & Ted's Excellent Video Game Adventure (NES)

This is one of the worst games on the NES.

You bounce around time zones grabbing items and there's no logic to any of it. No map, no direction, no hint that you're doing the right thing. Rufus is the only one who tells you anything and it still isn't enough.

9. Beetlejuice (NES)

Influence is not always positive.

Acclaim bought LJN in 1990 and kept putting that rainbow on licensed games for five more years. 

Beetlejuice was one of the first ones out the door under Acclaim, and it played like every joke people make about the logo.

Thirty five years later the rainbow is still an insult. That is influence.

10. NARC (NES)

The D.A.R.E. era pressed into a cartridge. 

1988, Nancy Reagan on every TV, "Just Say No" on every classroom wall, and Williams Electronics builds an arcade game where you play a cop who shoots drug dealers and drives over the bodies. 

Acclaim brought it into the house. Bad port of a game that was already mean. But it is a perfect fossil. 

You cannot explain 1990 to someone without explaining that a kid could rent this.

8. Double Dragon II: The Revenge (NES)

Before Streets of Rage, before Turtles in Time, this is what a beat em up meant in a living room.

Two players, one couch, one guy elbowing the other guy off a ledge on purpose. The entire genre's living room grammar starts here. 

Technos built it. Acclaim put it in the house.

Nintendo put Mario's name on it because Mario sells, and thirty years later people are still measuring it against a game it wasn't trying to be. It's not a sequel. It's barely the same genre.

I'll say the rest of it plainly: This is one of my all time favorite games. My mom helped me beat every Mario game I owned before this one. Yoshi's Island is the first one I finished by myself.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (N64)

I'm just going to say it:

This is the most overrated game ever made.

It's a good game. I replayed it recently, start to finish, as an adult. That's where this review is coming from, because I don't think most of the people calling it the greatest game ever made have played it since they were kids.

Go back to it now and the first thing that hits you is how much of this game is spent running across nothing. Hyrule Field is a big empty rectangle with a few Peahats and some holes in it, and you cross it constantly.

And before you ever get out there you're stuck doing errands in Kokiri Forest with Navi talking the whole time, because you can't even get into the Deku Tree until you've got the sword and the shield.

Forest Temple is great. Fire Temple is hallways.

Then there's the Water Temple. It isn't hard. The puzzles are fine. The problem is the iron boots, which you need to sink and walk underwater, are an equipment item buried in a pause menu, so the dungeon becomes pause, equip boots, walk, pause, unequip boots, swim, over and over for an hour. Even Nintendo admits this one. 

Eiji Aonuma, who directed the dungeon and went on to run the entire Zelda series, publicly apologized for it years later, and the 3DS remake moved the boots to a touch screen button so you'd never have to open the menu. When the guy who built it says sorry, it's not just me being contrarian.

The story is thinner than people remember too. Ganondorf gets everything he wants the second you pull the Master Sword, and then he basically disappears for the entire adult half of the game while you work down a checklist of five sages, one per dungeon, until the game decides you're allowed to fight him. There's no real second act.

What people are actually remembering is the music, and to be fair, the music deserves it. Gerudo Valley, Song of Storms, the Lost Woods. Koji Kondo put one of the best soundtracks ever made on that cartridge and I won't argue with anyone about that. But a great soundtrack wrapped around a thin story is still a thin story.

What Ocarina actually earned is Z-targeting. Before this game, nobody had really figured out how to fight in 3D. Ocarina solved it by letting you lock onto an enemy so the camera holds on them while you circle, strafe, and block. 

That system is basically in every 3D action game since. That's the real legacy, and it's a bigger one than the story or the world ever was.

Mario Kart peaked in 1992.

You press start and you're racing. No opening movie, no tutorial, no drivers to unlock, no menu asking what kind of experience you want.

The coins are the part everybody forgot.

No blue shell.

Battle mode is the other half of it. Three balloons, a flat square, and whatever the item box gives you. 

Thirty four years of bigger arenas and better graphics and none of it improved on battle mode.

Double Dash is the second best one and it's not close. Two characters, the item swap, a co-op idea nobody has touched since.

It follows the movie pretty closely, which is very surprising because video game movie tie-ins almost never follow the movie with any accuracy. It's usually just a label slapped on some generic thing (looking at you, Friday the 13th and Bill and Ted!)

The game starts with the Red Triangle Circus Gang crashing the tree lighting in Gotham Plaza and ends with Batman fighting the Penguin in his lair. Catwoman shows up on occasion to fight you along the way.

Between stages you get movie stills to carry the story.

The fighting mechanics are fantastic. You can grab two clowns at once and smash their heads together, or pick one up and throw him right through a store window. There's a Batmobile stage in the middle of the game too.

The music, the sound effects and the overall ambiance are absolutely stellar. 

Konami got Danny Elfman's score from the movie onto the cartridge, and the whole game has the same snowy Gotham at Christmas feel Tim Burton put on screen.

It's one of the best licensed games from the 16-bit era, and it ranks pretty high on my all time lists.

I rate Batman Returns on the Super Nintendo a 4.5 out of 5.

Disney Epic Mickey: Rebrushed (Xbox)

I completed Epic Mickey: Rebrushed yesterday.

The game came out in 2024, and most critics gave it a 7 or an 8. It’s sitting in the mid 70s on Metacritic.

Those critics are wrong.

This looks like a kid’s game until you play it. The story is dark and grim, with the whole game basically taking place at a post apocalyptic Disneyland. Running around the Wasteland and seeing the ruins of the animatronics all across the park, some of it had me thinking, “What game am I playing?” Some of it was really dark, and I loved it.

The gameplay is smooth with simple fight mechanics. It’s a very pro-player game. Lose a heart? Smash open a box and the game supplies you with another one.

The game wants you to win.

It wants you to have fun.

Pretty much everything in the game can be fixed with paint or wiped out with thinner, even some of the bosses. Paint an enemy and they turn into your friend. Their reactions after that got a chuckle out of me. Whatever you pick, the game remembers it. The characters treat you differently because of it, all the way to the ending.

You also fight a robot Captain Hook, right after running into Pete from A Goofy Movie dressed up as Peter Pan.

The music pulls from some of Disney’s most famous movies. The Fantasia level is fantastic. Hard to not hum along to the theme as you’re rushing through Yen Sid’s lab while the brooms are flooding the place.

One of the best Easter eggs I’ve ever seen in a video game is in this one, with Super Nintendo carts of “The Magical Quest” sitting in the ruins. Capcom released it in 1992, and it was awesome seeing the oversized cartridges lying in the toxic sludge.

It’s not often I call a game a masterpiece, but this one is a masterpiece.

Here's my Street Fighter (2026) review. 

I’m just going to say it: the 1994 Street Fighter movie was better. A coked out Jean-Claude Van Damme made more sense than what we got in 2026.

The critics were mostly right about this new one. It’s a mess, and a lot of the time it plays like a caricature of itself. 

I didn’t hate it though. Most of the movie was enjoyable.

The first 30 minutes had me thinking this was going to be one of the greatest video game movies ever made. Then it drops off and doesn’t really pick back up until the end.

The animated scenes were actually the best part of the movie.

The problem is they’re serious and dark, while the rest of the movie is goofy, over the top, and colorful, so they clash with the campiness of everything else.

The pacing was all over the place, same with the story, with too many fights happening off screen and a lot of it just not making any sense.

Some of the character choices were questionable. Guile was nothing like his character in the games. He was obnoxious and over the top, and he was barely in the movie. Same with E. Honda and Zangief.

Then there’s Lord Bison. No disrespect to the actor who played him, but he was the least intimidating villain of all time. This is one of the worst casting choices ever. Also, why did they turn Bison into a perv? Why is he always smelling people? It’s weird. His “Tuesday” line was so forced and out of place. He was the worst part of the movie.

The music selection was weird to me too. Most of the movie takes place in 1993, so why is “Who Let the Dogs Out” by the Baha Men playing? That song didn’t come out until 2000.

And the Marvel style forced humor was in every scene. Every line in this movie was someone trying to land a joke.

Chun-Li and Evil Ryu were the best characters in it, and along with the animated scenes, they’re the reason I didn’t walk out of there hating it.

It’s an entertaining watch, but that’s as far as I’d go with it. 

This one gets a 2/5 from me.

I still remember this vividly, like it just happened yesterday.

I grew up in Stockton, CA, not that far from San Francisco. I had just turned 6 years old, and my grandmother and I had just gotten home from school. I was in the kitchen sitting at the table working on my homework when the earthquake hit.

I had no idea what was going on or what to even do. I remember my grandmother yelling from the other side of the house for me to get under the table, but I didn’t listen.

The quake felt like it lasted for an eternity.

My grandpa was in a hurry to get home from work so he could watch the Giants and A’s in the World Series. I remember him saying he felt the quake while he was driving on the freeway.

Luckily, nothing in my grandparents’ house was damaged and we were all fine.

Honest and Unpopular Reviews No. 59

Max Payne 3 (Xbox 360)

Ask most people for Rockstar’s best game and it’s GTA V or Red Dead Redemption 2. I just played Max Payne 3 and I’m picking this one over anything Rockstar has ever made.

There’s no slowdown when you’re playing. Once this game begins, it’s just wave after wave of enemies. The story keeps bringing it. Red Dead Redemption 2 is the exact opposite: you have to go out and find the action in that one. 

The story in this game is fantastic. Max is a washed up drunk working private security for a rich family in São Paulo, at least until his boss’s wife gets kidnapped on his watch. The game keeps jumping back to how he got to Brazil in the first place, all the way back to New Jersey.

The soundtrack is one of the best I’ve ever heard in a game. It was done by a band called HEALTH.

The airport scene is one of the best scenes I’ve ever played in any video game ever made. The amount of enemies that come at you with that music playing, it’s its own vibe.

Bullet time is back from the first two games. So is the shootdodge. Drop the last guy in a fight and the camera follows the bullet all the way in, every time. Your health doesn’t come back on its own either. That’s what the painkillers are for (go down with one left and you get one last shot at whoever got you).

One thing I really liked in this game is it wants you to keep progressing.

A few parts of it are legitimately tough. There were a few times I kept dying in the same spot, and the game would give me extra painkillers and ammo.

The only knock on this game is the cutscenes. Well, not the cutscenes themselves, more how often they show up. You get 20 seconds of action and then a 3 minute cutscene you can’t skip that’s really just the game loading the next scene.

Despite being 14 years old, it holds up better than most of what’s coming out now.

I rate Max Payne 3 a 4.5 out of 5.

Honest and Unpopular Reviews No. 60

Sony PlayStation 2

The best selling console of all time is only the second best console ever made.

Sony sold over 160 million of them, more than any other console ever made.

It came out here on October 26, 2000 for $299, and good luck getting one that day. Sony was supposed to have a million ready for launch. A parts shortage cut that in half, so most of the people in line that morning went home with nothing.

I didn’t buy this console until 2008, when I was in the Navy, wanting to play Guitar Hero, MGS 2 and 3, and LEGO Batman. I bought the satin silver slim PS2 from the Navy Exchange on base.

I played it nonstop during my free time after I bought it. I used to have Guitar Hero parties in my barracks room. It was good times.

Most people bought this for a cheap DVD player. Back then $299 was less than a lot of actual DVD players cost.

Most of the library was shovelware. Over 4,000 games came out for it.

The Dreamcast had a modem in the box when it came out in 1999 for $199. If you wanted to play online on a PS2, you had to go buy a separate network adapter. That didn’t even show up here until August 2002, almost three years after the Dreamcast.

Overall, this console didn’t do anything special that the Dreamcast didn’t already do.

I rate the second greatest console of all time a 4.5 out of 5.
